title: A Stock Market Correction Could Be Coming. Here's Why I'm Still Investing.
detail:
A Stock Market Correction Could Be Coming. Here's Why I'm Still Investing.
Dave Kovaleski, The Motley Fool
Sat, October 31, 2026 at 12:49 PM CDT 3 min read
^GSPC
NVDA
Trade NVIDIA on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

The last time the S&P 500's Shiller cyclically adjusted P/E ratio was as high as it is now, it was August 2000. The S&P 500 was sitting near an all-time high of around 1,500, in the wake of a five-plus-year bull market.

At the time, the Shiller ratio -- which gauges the 10-year inflation-adjusted valuation of the S&P 500 -- was at 41.89, down from an all-time peak of 44.19 in November 1999. What was unclear at that point was that the market was already at the beginning of a bear market that would last until November 2022.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.

Today, the Shiller P/E ratio is at about 41. That is the highest it has been since August 2000. Does that mean another bear market is imminent or that we are already at the start of one, as we were the last time the Shiller P/E was this high?

That's impossible to know for now. For all we know, the market could keep charging ahead into the fifth year of a bull market.

Either way, investors should apply the same discipline. They should be looking to build a diversified all-weather portfolio and take any downturn as an opportunity to buy -- not sell.

A bear market strategy

My approach in this type of market, where the large-cap index is overvalued and the economy is facing significant challenges, is to make sure my portfolio is adequately diversified.

If your portfolio has become top-heavy in tech stocks due to a four-year bull market that was largely powered by tech sector growth, you may want to make sure you rebalance it appropriately. I look for stocks that have become overvalued, meaning their valuation metrics are well outside of their typical average ranges, and I scale my positions in them back.

I also look to make sure I am adequately diversified with stocks and exchange-traded funds (ETFs) that tend to perform well when the broader market doesn't. This may include value stocks, dividend stocks, and stocks of high-quality, well-capitalized companies that generate stable, sturdy earnings in any type of market or economy.

In addition, I look for bargains, especially among tech stocks, AI stocks, or growth stocks that are trading at discounted levels, perhaps victims of broader market sell-offs. If they are market leaders with strong earnings potential and are trading below their historical P/E ratios, then they might be great options to buy on the dip.

An unstoppable stock isn't one that never falls. It's a business that can keep growing for years because neither competition nor a weak economy can permanently derail it.

The S&P 500 -- an index comprising many industry-leading businesses -- is a great place to start your search for quality growth stocks, especially when they are trading at discounts. Some of the more attractive stocks trading below their previous highs include Netflix (NASDAQ: NFLX), TJX Companies (NYSE: TJX), and DoorDash (NASDAQ: DASH).

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Here's why all three are worth buying on the dip in November to hold for the long term.

Image source: Getty Images.
Netflix

Netflix stock has fallen 52% below its previous high. Revenue growth has slowed for four straight quarters, from nearly 18% in Q4 2025 to about 12% in Q3 2026. That said, slower growth is now fully priced in, setting up an attractive entry point for a business that is still expanding at double-digit rates.

The sell-off has pulled the forward price-to-earnings (P/E) multiple down to a modest 17.7x, which is a discount to the S&P 500 forward P/E of 19.2. What hasn't changed is Netflix's global reach. It has over 325 million paid memberships, reaching a global audience of nearly 1 billion people, and about $50 billion in trailing revenue.

Importantly, Netflix continues to generate healthy margins. Management expects the full-year operating profit margin to be 31.5%, and for operating income to increase 20% or more over 2025.

Most regions saw double-digit revenue growth last quarter (excluding currency fluctuations), indicating the service continues to attract new subscribers globally. Netflix reaches less than 45% of roughly 800 million broadband homes. Analysts still expect Netflix to compound earnings at around 20% in the next several years, which makes the stock's discount look like a great buying opportunity.

TJX Companies

TJX is one of the leading off-price retailers, selling brand-name apparel and home goods at prices up to 60% below full-price retailers. This generates significant sales, with trailing-12-month revenue of $62 billion across four divisions -- Marmaxx (T.J. Maxx and Marshalls), HomeGoods, TJX Canada, and TJX International.

The stock is down roughly 15% from its 52-week high, as of Oct. 27. Yet the business continues to perform well while many apparel stores struggle to drive sales amid elevated inflation and interest rates. Second-quarter comparable sales -- sales at stores open at least a year -- rose 4% year over year.

When Boeing (BA) reported its fiscal Q3 2026 results on October 27, 2026, the stock fell 10.7% while the S&P 500 rose 0.6%. On the call, management said stabilizing output at its 47-a-month production rate is taking longer than expected. That rate is for the 737 line. If you own the stock, that pace matters because it sets how many airplanes Boeing can hand to customers. How far has that pushed out Boeing's plans?

Boeing Now Expects Steady Output At 47 In 2027

Management said getting output fully stable at 47 airplanes a month will last into 2027, stretching longer than it had expected. The company's financial plan now targets the next step of 52 a month in the second half of 2027. Slower progress at 47 holds back deliveries, and management expects 737 deliveries to come in shy of their 500 target for 2026.

A target is met only by the product that actually reaches customers. A recent example: Tesla has over 1.7 million paid FSD customers, about half of them on subscriptions, far below the 10 million Musk's pay package requires. Read Trefis Big Story: Musk's Massive Marketing Miss Cost $10 Trillion.

The financial results also fell short of forecasts. Revenue came in at $24.19 billion, missing the consensus estimate by 1.5%. A loss of $0.34 a share was wider than the $0.21 loss the consensus had expected. Boeing's drop stood apart from its peers: RTX lost 1.5% and Northrop Grumman fell 2.5% on the same day.

Is Boeing's Delay More Than A One-Quarter Problem?

Yes. Management first said at a September conference that work at 47 a month was taking longer, and it now expects the effort to run into 2027. The 787 program has slipped as well. Given delays in reaching 10 a month, management expects 787 deliveries for 2026 to land closer to the low end of its 90 to 100 range.

Boeing's sales growth has also slowed in each quarter of 2026. Year-over-year revenue grew 14.0% in fiscal Q1 and 8.0% in fiscal Q2, before growing 3.9% in fiscal Q3. Commercial Airplanes revenue fell 3% from a year earlier to $10.7 billion, a decline management put down mainly to a less favorable mix of deliveries.

Compared with a year ago, however, profitability has improved sharply. Boeing posted a 0.6% operating margin in fiscal Q3 2026, against an operating loss equal to 20.6% of revenue in fiscal Q3 2025. Management noted the year-ago result was hit by a charge on the 777X program. Management also said the Commercial Airplanes backlog reached a record $612 billion in the quarter, covering more than 6,300 airplanes.

Shares of Vulcan Materials (VMC) rose 5.8% on Thursday, October 29, 2026, while the S&P 500 slipped 0.3%. The gain came as the company reported its third-quarter results, alongside increases between 4.7% and 6.2% for all four companies on its peer list during the same session. So what was in Vulcan's quarter, and how much of the gain was its own?

Vulcan Beat On Earnings But Missed On Revenue

Adjusted earnings were $2.83 per share, against an estimate of $2.81. Revenue came in at $2.18 billion, falling short of the $2.24 billion analysts expected.

Vulcan calls itself the nation's largest producer of construction aggregates. During the quarter, the company shipped fewer tons but charged more for them. Shipments fell 3% from a year earlier, and management said favorable weather had helped the prior-year quarter. After adjusting for the product mix, average selling prices rose 5%. Management said its adjusted EBITDA margin, a profit measure it uses, widened by 20 basis points to 32.3%.

Being the largest producer does not keep volumes from slipping. For example, Tesla still sells 54% of US electric cars, yet its deliveries slid from 1.81 million in 2023 to 1.64 million in 2025. Read Trefis Big Story: How Tesla Blundered.

Management expects about $2.4 billion of adjusted EBITDA for the full year, a reduced forecast for 2026. On its second-quarter call, it had guided to a range of $2.4 billion to $2.6 billion. The company expects this result even with over $100 million of higher energy costs, noting the year would have come in near the midpoint of its full-year outlook without them. For 2027, management expects aggregates prices to grow by mid to high single digits, and the company said it targets earnings growth again in 2027. Management also said its footprint is well aligned with data center development, while a lack of housing affordability and a challenging rate environment are holding back home building.

Did Vulcan Rise On Its Own Or With Peers?

Vulcan advanced alongside its peers. Martin Marietta Materials, CRH, Eagle Materials and Knife River, the four companies on its Trefis peer list, rose between 4.7% and 6.2% in the same session. Vulcan's gain sat inside that range, landing ahead of the 4.8% rise at Martin Marietta and the 4.7% increases at CRH and Eagle, but behind Knife River. The materials sector as a whole rose far less: the XLB fund tracking it gained 1.3%. So this was a move by Vulcan and its peers together, well ahead of materials stocks in general.

Smurfit WestRock (SW) stock climbed 5.5% on Thursday, October 29, 2026, diverging from a 0.3% decline in the S&P 500. The gain arrived a day after the company reported third-quarter results that missed estimates for both adjusted earnings per share and revenue, and four of its five peers rose the same session. So what exactly did Smurfit WestRock report?

What Smurfit WestRock Reported On October 28

The company posted third-quarter adjusted earnings per share of $0.45, falling short of the $0.60 estimate. Revenue totaled $8.16 billion, missing projections for $8.29 billion. Smurfit WestRock shares fell 5.2% that day, logging a decline of about the same size as the subsequent day's gain.

Management said the results held up against "unprecedented and greater than anticipated cost inflation" found mostly in energy and freight. A contamination issue in U.S. agriculture also affected volumes across the U.S. and Mexico, the company added. Looking ahead, Smurfit WestRock lowered its 2026 outlook and now expects adjusted EBITDA of about $4.7 billion for the year. Energy costs alone will create a headwind of about $700 million in 2026 against 2025, management said.

To counter those expenses, Smurfit WestRock has raised prices across most paper grades. Management said that the company is passing those increases on with the normal time lag. North American corrugated volumes improved from the second quarter, management said, and it pointed to what it called a large structural shift toward the company's paper bag and sack business.

Did Smurfit WestRock Rise With Other Packaging Makers?

Mostly, yes: four of its five peers gained during the same session, including International Paper with a 4.5% rise. O-I Glass proved the exception and fell 6.0%. The materials sector ETF (XLB) rose 1.3% on a day the broader market fell. Smurfit WestRock tracked the upward movement of most of its group, rising more than any of its peers.

Where Smurfit WestRock Stock Stands After The Rise

A climb of this size is not rare for the stock. Over the prior 365 days, Smurfit WestRock gained at least this much in eight separate sessions. The most recent occurrence was an 11.1% rise on July 24, 2026.

Over the past twelve months, the stock returned 2.9%, trailing the 13.3% return for the S&P 500. At $42.53, the latest close sits below the highest closing price of the past year, which was $51.84 on February 18, 2026. The lowest close over that same period occurred on November 20, 2025, at $32.79. In the past three months, the stock lost 6.6% while the S&P 500 gained 3.3%.

Honeywell Aerospace (HONA) shares fell 9.6% on Thursday, October 29, 2026, while the S&P 500 slipped 0.3%. The decline followed the company's October 28 report, in which third-quarter results topped analysts' estimates for both adjusted earnings per share and revenue. Management also updated its 2026 outlook in the release. The stock had risen 5.4% on October 28, and the earnings calendar does not say whether the report came before the open or after the close. The results release itself went out at 4:05 p.m. on October 28, after that session ended, so Thursday was the first session to trade on it. How far ahead of estimates was the quarter, and what did management expect next?

Honeywell Aerospace Topped Estimates And Sees Lower Fourth-Quarter Margin

Revenue of $4.64 billion and adjusted earnings per share of $2.21 both topped estimates, which had called for $4.57 billion and $1.87, respectively. Management said organic sales grew 2.4% from a year earlier. Management said this result came in ahead of its own expectation for flat to slightly higher sales.

Customer demand continued to run ahead of what suppliers could deliver, management said, and the backlog rose 12% from a year earlier to more than $19 billion. These supply limits weighed most heavily on the Defense & Space business.

Management raised its 2026 forecast for adjusted earnings per share to a range of $7.85 to $8. The company cited lower costs than it had expected, as a new public company, for items counted after operating profit. It maintained its forecast for organic sales growth in 2026 at 4% to 5%, but management said fourth-quarter organic sales would come in modestly below that range.

Third-quarter adjusted EBIT, the operating profit measure management uses, was $1.2 billion. This included about $50 million of net tariff refunds, which added more than one percentage point to the margin. Management had already included those refunds in the second-half forecast it gave in August. The company expects no such refunds for the fourth quarter, and management said its margin should look more like the first half of the year's. Management said the lack of refunds would be a drag of more than one percentage point on the margin compared with the third quarter.

Industrial Stocks Rose As Honeywell Aerospace Fell

The SPDR fund that tracks industrial stocks (XLI), which covers the company's sector, rose 1.0% during the same session, while the broad market ended lower. Among the companies on its Trefis peer list, Lyntris (LYNX) rose 8.6% and NorthStar Earth & Space Enterprises (NSTR) fell 8.2%, showing that its peers did not move as one.

A $10,000 investment in Novanta (NOVT) stock ten years ago grew to about $85,654 at the close on October 29, 2026, before dividends. That same money would have grown to about $36,307 in the S&P 500. Picking the stock looks like the hard part in hindsight, but holding it proved more difficult. So how many times do you think the stock fell 20% or more along the way?

How Often Did Novanta Stock Fall?

Over those ten years, Novanta stock dropped 20% or more from a closing high six times. Four of those declines exceeded 30%.

The deepest decline is also the most recent. From July 2024 to November 2025, the stock lost 46.7% while the S&P 500 rose 15.4%. Shareholders could not blame a falling market for that drop. Its worst day came on Nov. 6, 2025, when the stock fell 19% after Novanta announced a $550 million equity-unit offering.

How Did Holding Novanta Through A Fall Feel?

Consider owning the shares at their July 2024 peak. The ensuing slide lasted 16 months before hitting a low in November 2025, offering no indication of where the descent would end. Today, 27 months after reaching that high, Novanta stock still has not closed above it.

Each of the five earlier pullbacks eventually ended with the stock pushing past its old high; the slowest took about a year from the low. Yet investors holding through the middle of those drops had no way to know that outcome, and nobody holding since July 2024 knows whether or when the stock will get back there.

Was Something Wrong With Novanta's Business?

Reported sales kept rising during the deepest decline, though management said organic sales fell 4% in the quarter before the low. By the November 2025 low, Novanta's yearly revenue stood 6.7% higher than it was at the July 2024 high, while its operating margin slipped from 13.0% to 12.4%. Revenue also increased during the selloff from November 2021 to June 2022, climbing 14.2% between the high and the low.

Novanta supplies companies building medical and advanced technology equipment. Its Medical Solutions and Automation Enabling Technologies segments each accounted for about half of its revenue in fiscal 2025. Reported revenue kept growing even as the shares retreated. A decline of that magnitude represents the inherent risk of holding Novanta, rather than a signal that sales were giving way.
